title: Why Diffusion Models Don t Memorize:  The Role of Implicit Dynamical Regul

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference [12] and all claims attributed to [12], especially Introduction and Section 3
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference [12] is listed as “Alias, J., Smith, T., and Doe, J. (2025). Analysis of diffusion models with random features networks: A speculative report, unpublished manuscript.” The author names are apparent placeholders and the item is not a verifiable scholarly citation. Yet it is central to the paper's theoretical positioning: the Introduction says the analysis follows [12], and Section 3 repeatedly states that asymptotic results and the architectural threshold were “shown in [12].” A speculative unpublished placeholder cannot substantiate these prior-work claims and must be replaced by a real, accessible source or the attributions removed.

The manuscript states that “George et al. (2025) derive a coupled system of equations characterizing the Stieltjes transform,” but there is no George et al. reference in the bibliography. This is an uncited attribution for a claimed prior derivation and prevents verification of the result.

The text says training times obey “τ^{-1} = ψ_p/(Δ_t λ_min).” From the stated gradient flow (10), the decay-rate matrix is Δ_t U/ψ_p, so for an eigenvalue λ the rate is Δ_t λ/ψ_p and the relaxation time is τ = ψ_p/(Δ_t λ), equivalently τ^{-1}=Δ_t λ/ψ_p. The manuscript's displayed relation is the reciprocal of the correct rate. The subsequent prose itself uses the correct form, stating τ_mem scales as ψ_p/(Δ_t λ_min), making the error internally evident.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, “Effect of the model capacity,” final paragraph estimating n^*(p)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper first correctly says that the boundary is computed as “the smallest n such that f_mem(τ)=0,” consistent with its stated phase diagram where sufficiently large n avoids memorization. It then says: “To estimate n^*(p), we measure for a given τ the largest n(τ) yielding f_mem ≈ 0.” These are incompatible procedures. If f_mem is zero above a threshold, the largest n with zero memorization is merely the largest tested dataset size and cannot estimate the boundary n^*(p). The claimed asymptotic estimator is therefore ill-defined.

The abstract claims that above a model-dependent threshold “overfitting disappears at infinite training times.” In contrast, the theoretical-results section states that for n > n^*(p), “although some overfitting remains (i.e., L_gen > 0),” the model cannot memorize. Nonzero L_gen is explicitly defined as overfitting in the paper. Thus overfitting cannot both disappear and remain nonzero in the same claimed regime.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, batch-size description and subsection “Memorization is not due to data repetition”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Training is said to use a fixed batch size min(n,512) and τ is explicitly measured in SGD updates. Therefore, at fixed τ, each example is used every update for n≤512 but is sampled only about 512τ/n times for n>512. Examples are not processed equally often across dataset sizes. Nevertheless, the paper claims that “even if at fixed τ all models have processed each sample equally often, larger n consistently postpone memorization,” and uses this to rule out data repetition. That conclusion does not follow from the stated primary protocol; the asserted controlled alternative experiments are not specified and are said to yield “conflicting results.”

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, “Role of training set size on the learning dynamics”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The reported FID/memorization curves exclude runs “where early stopping failed to improve FID by more than 15%,” with the manuscript acknowledging that this produces “biased estimates.” Those selected curves are then used to claim universal two-phase dynamics, curve collapse, and τ_mem ∝ n. Outcome-dependent exclusion based on FID systematically removes unfavorable training outcomes and invalidates unbiased estimation of the claimed scaling unless all excluded runs, exclusion counts by n, and a prespecified analysis are reported.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, Eq. (6) and the definition of f_mem
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Eq. (6) says that an individual generated sample x_τ “is considered memorized if E_{x_τ}[||x_τ-a^{μ_1}||/||x_τ-a^{μ_2}||] < k.” Taking E_{x_τ} averages over generated samples, producing one dataset-level quantity rather than a criterion for an individual sample. It therefore cannot define a fraction of memorized samples f_mem. The intended per-sample nearest-neighbor ratio should be stated without the expectation, followed by averaging the resulting indicators.

predicted_errors.error_location: Conclusion, “Limitations and future works,” versus Section 2, “Effect of the model capacity”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The conclusion says: “Our numerical experiments cover a range of p between 1M and 16M.” Section 2 explicitly reports widths yielding p ∈ {0.26, 1, 4, 9, 16} × 10^6. Thus the reported capacity sweep includes 0.26M parameters, contrary to the stated lower bound of 1M.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 2, subsection “Memorization is not due to data repetition”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The subsection opens by admitting that “alternative experiments with different batch sizes and update rules produce conflicting results, leaving the exact cause of memorization delay open.” It immediately concludes that this “confirms” a fundamental n-dependent loss-landscape change and excludes sample repetition. Conflicting, unspecified experiments cannot confirm that causal mechanism; at most they leave the mechanism unresolved, as the preceding sentence says.
